summary: Independent second verification of 10 batch numbers; all work was done from the Internet Archive scan and its OCR, with nothing in the repo modified. Entries 1241, 1328, 1428, 1498, 1529, 1596, 1684 and 1714 are page pointers into OR Ser. I vol. 27 pt. 3 (the list's Part XIII). For each I fetched the Internet Archive scan (warofrebellion273unit, Univ. of Illinois copy, title page "Government Printing Office 1889"). I mapped printed page to leaf with the Archive's page_numbers.json (leaf = printed + 6) and read the page image, folio, running head and text. I did not fetch eHistory: its robots.txt request already returned a Cloudflare 403 challenge, so I stopped there. Instead I read Wayback Machine captures of each listed eHistory URL (8 of 8 exist, 2021-2025, web.archive.org robots.txt returns 404): every capture is "Serial 045 Page NNNN" with the page named, so the targets are right at capture time. All 8 are A1 (US Government work, 1889 imprint). They are valid page pointers, but they are link-out/cross-check items, not quote sources. The linked eHistory transcription is lossy (details below). Where the list says anything specific, it holds up: the Birney July 7 dispatch on p.586, the roster on p.1029 and the organization table on p.1059 are all as described. Two descriptions are wrong: p.673 has no dispatches (it is a plate of two sketches), and p.843 is Union only (the 'section transition' label is false). I agree with the first pass (APPROVE-LINKOUT-ONLY, A1) on all 8 real entries. I disagree on 1718 and 1722: the list has no such entries. The source document and entries.json end at n=1714 (p.1059); the numbers are page+655 extrapolations. Pages 1063 and 1067 themselves exist and are A1, but nothing in the list points to them. I mark both NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW so a builder does not create approvals for non-existent entries; they should simply be dropped. Not verified: the live eHistory/HathiTrust links (blocked to bots), and the HathiTrust seq offsets (no entry in this batch carries a HathiTrust link).
systemic_findings: Entries 1718 and 1722 do not exist: docs/historian/sources-v2 entries.json, the parsed raw text and the registry all end at n=1714 (OR vol. 27 pt. 3 p.1059), and the numbers equal printed page + 655 (1241=p.586 ... 1714=p.1059). Whoever built this batch extrapolated beyond the list; the first-pass APPROVE-LINKOUT-ONLY for them should be discarded. Pages 1060-1068 and the rest of the volume are simply not in the list.

eHistory (ehistory.osu.edu) returns a Cloudflare managed-challenge 403 even for /robots.txt; nothing further was requested from it. Wayback Machine captures exist for all 8 listed eHistory URLs and show 'Serial 045 Page NNNN' with the same page and text, so the 8 page pointers are correct (at capture time, 2021-2025). Wayback's own robots.txt returned 404 (no restrictions).

The eHistory transcription is not verbatim. Evidence: p.843 footnote reads 'August 18, p. 841' in the scan image but 'August 28' in the capture; p.1059 omits the printed line '8th Georgia, Col. John R. Towers.'; p.773 has 'chef engineer'; p.673 shows only 'MAP'. It should not be a quote source: quote from the Archive scan/OCR (and check the image), and use eHistory only as a link-out.

Historian OCR ingestion defects found while checking this batch, directly from scan evidence: (1) or27-3:p0673.1-.5 are actually on printed p.674 (leaf 680); p.673 is a two-sketch plate with no text, and p.674 has no row. This also makes the registry structural check for entry 1328 rest on mis-paged rows. (2) or27-3:p0586.4 has signer G. K. WARREN but the dispatch (Hdqrs. Eleventh Army Corps, July 7, 9 p.m.) is signed O. O. HOWARD at the top of p.587; place OCR 'Mechcmicstown' in p0586.1. (3) or27-3:p1029.1 and p1067.1 are table headings read as dispatches (addressee 'Brig. Gen. Henry A. Wise.', place 'C. S. Army, commanding', date '1863-07-81'). (4) p0843.1 is only the August 3, 1863 inclosure; the December 6, 1878 Meigs letter has no row.

Two-column organization tables (pp.1029, 1059, 1063, 1067) are linearised column by column in the Archive OCR, with headings grouped away from their unit lines. Example: Law's and Benning's brigades follow the 'RODES' DIVISION' heading in the text but are printed in Hood's division. The first pass repeated this misreading ('Rodes's division with Law's, Benning's ...'). Such pages need layout-aware or manual handling.

Union/Confederate boundary in Part 3 verified from running heads: Union heads on pp.5-857, the Union Addenda start on p.843 ('ADDENDA.' printed after Le Duc's letter), and 'CONFEDERATE CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.' appears first on p.858. So the 'Union / Confederate (section transition)' label for p.843 is false; p.843 is Union only.

Page mapping for this volume is stable: printed page = Archive leaf - 6 and image index nNNN = printed + 5, with image checks at pp.586, 672, 673, 843, 1059, 1067. IA metadata shows date '1880' (the series' first year) while the printed title page says 1889; imprint and public-domain status are unaffected. The Archive copy is a University of Illinois copy with the note 'Some content affected by narrow inner margins', while the HathiTrust record the registry cites for Part 3 (coo.31924077700262, rightsCode pd, Full view) is Cornell's copy: same edition, different scan.

Nothing was written to the repo or committed; scratch files (Archive OCR, page images, Wayback captures) are under the session scratchpad directory .../scratchpad/v2nd3/. Requests: archive.org (metadata, page numbers, OCR, page images, page-view URLs, availability API), web.archive.org captures, one HathiTrust catalog API record, one eHistory robots.txt request, all with the honest User-Agent at no more than 1 request per second per host.

summary: Independent second-verifier pass over entries 581, 582, 583, 603, 607, 612, 615, 616 (all Part IX). Verdicts: APPROVE 581, 583, 607, 612, 616 (every one with an A2 rights hold); APPROVE-LINKOUT-ONLY 582, 603; NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW 615 (1933 imprint, tier unknown). I agree with the first pass on 7 of 8 verdicts; the one difference is 581, where I found a second Wayback capture of the PDF that is complete (5,068,054 bytes; the first pass saw a truncated copy) and could check the typed transcript against the manuscript scans. Other corrections to the first pass: 603's text layer for all 16 pages is recoverable from the 1 MiB-truncated capture (p. 19 is not missing); Stayman (607) graduated in 1841 per a live Dickinson page, so he is an older alumnus, not a student; Stayman's August 1863 letter is live on the new Dickinson site; 607's July transcript reads 'the 29th ult.' where the manuscript scan appears to read '27th'. Link status: 6 dead Dickinson URLs (301 to https, then 404), 2 redirects to generic landing pages (583 UVA/VOTS home, 612 Notre Dame home). Every description in this batch was inherited from Dickinson's catalogue tags or an index page and not from the text; 581 and 582 are materially wrong about Carlisle (their writer was not there for the occupation or shelling). Everything below was fetched or computed in this run (honest User-Agent, robots.txt obeyed, >=1.3 s per host, no browser, no Perseus/eHistory/HathiTrust); local evidence files are under tmp/sources-v2/v2b/out/. Not verified: the original manuscripts (all scans seen are Dickinson's or Notre Dame's), Himes's, Harris's and Stayman's death dates, Copyright Office renewal records for the 1933 pamphlet, any licence text beyond the footers and statements cited, Notre Dame's page images (not on Wayback under the path tried).
systemic_findings: Dickinson 'Civil War Resources' was removed in a site migration, not just re-slugged. The 2025 site menu no longer lists it (the 2024 Wayback menu did). Item URLs partly survive under /document-descriptions/<slug> and people pages under /archives-people/<slug>: the Stayman August 1863 letter is live there (with a live 2,062,386-byte PDF), and the Himes people page is live but lists no 1863 letter or diary; guessed slugs for Himes (Rood letter, pocket diary), Harris, Sullivan and the broadside returned 404. A blanket rewrite of the old URLs would give wrong or dead links; each Dickinson entry needs its own check.

Wayback PDF captures of Dickinson files are often cut at exactly 1,048,576 bytes (Harris diary 603, Stayman August letter 607 in the 2024 capture) while another capture of the same file can be complete (Himes letter 581: 20240225221947 about 1 MB versus 20240703042213, 5,068,054 bytes complete). Check the CDX 'length' column and fetch the largest capture before declaring a file truncated. Truncated linearized PDFs can still yield the whole text layer by inflating every content stream (tmp/sources-v2/v2b/pdftxt.py); poppler's pdftotext refuses them. The first pass's claims of missing pages for 581 and 603 came from this.

Wayback services flapped during this run (HTTP 503 'Temporarily Offline' on the CDX API, ECONNREFUSED on id_ fetches, one timeout); every fetch succeeded within five spaced retries. Results from one attempt should not be treated as a missing capture.

Part IX descriptions were taken from Dickinson's catalogue tags (Event/Incident, summary line), not from reading the items. Where the tags are wrong or generic the description is wrong: Himes diary tagged 'Shelling of Carlisle' (he left Carlisle on 25 June), Himes letter described as 'occupation and shelling' (he was not there), Stayman called a professor (not stated anywhere I read). Treat every Part IX description as a lead, not a fact.

Rights pattern for the Dickinson items: all carry an 'All rights reserved' footer and no licence; all underlying texts are 1863 private manuscripts whose authors died before 1956, except the 1933 Sullivan pamphlet; the host adds typed transcripts, editorial footnotes (603) and cover sheets. A single counsel decision about Dickinson's transcripts and scans would settle 581, 582, 603, 607 and 616 together. Valley of the Shadow adds an explicit UVA copyright and a non-commercial-use statement (583); Notre Dame adds a copyright notice on its 2004-06 transcription (612).

Dickinson's PDFs combine three things in different quality: manuscript scans (garbage OCR, discard), typed transcripts (usable text layer with scan noise and occasional transcription errors such as 'the 29th ult.' versus an apparent '27th' in 607) and a Dickinson cover page. Any ingest should take the typed transcript only after a check against the manuscript scans, and where no manuscript scan exists (582, 603) restrict use to facts and dates.

Sensitive language: 603 and 615 contain racial slurs in the source text; 603 and 612 describe enslaved or hired Black people and a slave's funeral; 581 mentions 'the negro population' impressed to dig rifle pits. Any quotation selection needs careful framing and a content review.

items.written: 1863-10-02 (dateline 'New Oxford Adams Co. Pa. Oct. 2nd, 1863'; about three months after the events)
items.rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 manuscript letter. Himes is 'Class of 1855' on Dickinson's own pages, so he was born about 1835-40 and cannot have been alive in 1956: the life+70 term for an unpublished pre-1978 work has expired (his exact death date was not fetched). Tier A2, not A1, because the host adds an 'All rights reserved' footer (Copyright 2014 on the 2015 capture, 2020 on later ones) and the Dickinson-made typed transcript and cover sheet are modern; no licence text exists on the item page, and the Archives' public Access Restrictions policy (fetched) covers access to college records, not reuse.
items.evidence: Listed URL http://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war/letter-charles-f-himes-ogden-n-rood: my fetch returned 301 to https then 404 'Page not found' (25,346 bytes). Wayback CDX shows captures 20150919055535 (200), 20200203180456 (404), 20240706130250 (301), 20240706132412 (404). Item page 20150919055535 (21,452 bytes) read: 'Letter from Charles F. Himes to Ogden N. Rood', 13 pages, Date October 2, 1863, Gift of Mary Himes Vale and Sarah Vale Rush, tags Battle of Gettysburg / Invasion of Carlisle / Invasion of Pennsylvania (no Shelling tag); its PDF link is archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/MC2000-1_b10_f10.pdf. That path has no capture; the same file under files_war/mc2000-01_b10_f10.pdf has two captures per CDX (20240225221947, 1,035,028 bytes; 20240703042213, 4,992,538 bytes). I fetched 20240703042213: 5,068,054 bytes, sha256 ebacbeef0a366cbe..., complete (cover sheet plus 12 page images: 6 manuscript sheets 2327x2913 and 6 typed transcript pages 2503x3241). Read the typed text (OCR layer, noisy) and compared with the manuscript scans on sheet 1 and the last sheet: they agree (sheet 1 'preferring to look the Johnnies in the eye'; last sheet 'a piece of fern for Mrs Rood from Round Top ... I have a Rebel bone'). Content checks of the entry's description: he writes from New Oxford, says he was in Carlisle for Commencement about 25 June, describes the alarm, rifle pits dug about a mile west of town by the 'negro population', citizen soldiers supported by 'two N. York militia regts', then says he and his brother drove home over the mountain; he was NOT in Carlisle for the occupation (27-30 June) or the shelling (1 July). The rest covers Gordon's brigade passing through New Oxford on Saturday 27 June, the Hanover cavalry fight 30 June ('Stuart in person charged on Gen. Kilpatrick's column'), walking 17 miles to Gettysburg on 1 July 'just after the Rebs had driven our men through the town', being turned back by a Confederate officer, Kilpatrick's column passing on 2 July, and the Round Top fern. Hence 'Carlisle civilian ... occupation and shelling of the town' is wrong on three counts (not a Carlisle resident, no occupation, no shelling). Himes is the Dickinson alumnus and later professor (Dickinson current people page: 'Professor Charles F. Himes, ... Class of 1855', LL.D. 1896).
items.extraction_notes: Use the complete PDF capture https://web.archive.org/web/20240703042213/https://archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/files_war/mc2000-01_b10_f10.pdf (pdftotext works). Pages 2-7 are manuscript images with an OCR layer that is garbage (discard); pages 8-13 are the typed transcript with a usable but noisy text layer (spurious spaces inside words, e.g. 't hat n i ght'): clean it and check every quote against the manuscript scans. Page breaks are marked '-2-'..'-6-' in the typed text. Segment by topic: Carlisle alarm (about 6 sentences), journey home, New Oxford 27 June, Hanover 30 June, Gettysburg 1-3 July, closing business. About 12 passages. The letter uses 'negro population' and 'Rebs'; frame carefully. Provenance line: Dickinson College Archives MC 2000.1, B10, F10.
issues: Description wrong: not a Carlisle civilian in the occupation; no occupation or shelling in the letter. Carlisle appears only 24-25 June (alarm, fortifications) before any Confederate arrived.
Writes from New Oxford, Adams County, where he lived; his firsthand material is Gordon's brigade at New Oxford (27 June), Hanover (30 June) and the road to Gettysburg (1-2 July).
Written three months after the events: close recollection, not same-day.

items.written: 1863-06-23 to 1863-07-03 (diary entries; the transcript is partial and ends on 3 July)
items.rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 diary; Himes, 'Class of 1855', was necessarily dead before 1956, so the text itself is out of copyright (death date not fetched). A2 because the only text is a modern typed partial transcript made by Dickinson (author not named, gaps and hand corrections), the host footer says 'Copyright 2020 ... All rights reserved', and Dickinson states a complete transcript 'is not yet available'.
items.evidence: Listed URL: 301 to https then 404 (my fetch, 25,359 bytes). Wayback item page 20240302072813 (22,446 bytes): 'Pocket Diary of Charles F. Himes', 3 pages, Date 1863, Location MC 2000.1, B16, F2, text 'Partial transcript included. A complete transcript for this diary is not yet available.', tags Battle of Gettysburg / Invasion of Carlisle / Shelling of Carlisle. PDF capture 20240620182659 (reached via the 2024 nearest-capture redirect; fetched after two refused connections): 968,550 bytes, sha256 bf38abddc70019d8..., cover sheet plus two page images (2400x3282, 2400x3075) of a typed transcript with hand corrections, with a text layer. I read the page image: entries Tuesday 23 June ('Drove over to Carlisle'), 24 June (rumour that Rebs were within 8 miles), 25 June (Commencement, 'Dispatch came that the rebs were within 4 miles', he and 'Lan' started home, got home 10:30 pm), Saturday 27 June headed '(New Oxford)' ('about 3,000 infantry Gordon's brigade, Early's Div. Ewell's Corps passed through, they fired the R.R. Bridge'), 30 June (cannonading toward Hanover), 1 July (went toward Gettysburg, 'Saw their amublences carrying off the dead and wounded', stayed 3 miles from town), 2 July (turned back by an officer), 3 July (heavy firing, left 'under fear of a flank movement'). So the description 'day-by-day civilian diary covering the Confederate presence in Carlisle' is wrong: Himes left Carlisle on 25 June, two days before the first Confederates arrived there; the Carlisle entries are pre-occupation and the Confederates he describes are at New Oxford and near Gettysburg. The 'Shelling of Carlisle' tag is not supported by the text.

items.written: 1863-06-28 (dateline 'Hd. Qrs. 2nd Corps A.N.V. Carlisle Pa.')
items.rights_basis: Underlying text: an 1863 private letter by Jedediah Hotchkiss (born 1828, so dead before 1956; death year not fetched), unpublished at the time; the host copy is a transcription made from microfilm. The TEI header of the document (fetched) carries 'Copyright (c) 2001 by the Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia', 'Used with permission from Library of Congress', source 'Jedediah Hotchkiss Collection, Reel 4, Manuscripts Division, Library of Congress'. The site's Copyright and Fair Use Statement (fetched) says the site is free for non-commercial research, teaching, scholarship and private study, asks for citation, and warns that some materials may still be under copyright. So the text is old but the transcription carries an explicit copyright claim and a non-commercial condition: A2, rights review before any verbatim use.
items.evidence: Listed URL http://valley.lib.virginia.edu/papers/A4042: my fetch got 301 to https://valley.lib.virginia.edu/papers/A4042, then 301 to https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/ (HTTP 200, 178,202 bytes, the generic Valley of the Shadow home page): a dead link in disguise. The same document is live at https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/letters/A4042 (200, 166,712 bytes; robots.txt on that host is an empty 404): 'Augusta County: Jedediah Hotchkiss to Sara A. Hotchkiss, June 28, 1863', summary 'Hotchkiss describes the people and provisions the Confederate Army finds in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, and the lack of military opposition in the vicinity'. TEI source fetched from api.valley.newamericanhistory.org/storage/data/papers/A4042.xml (10,357 bytes, robots 'Disallow:' empty). Two description checks against the text: (1) the writer is Ewell's Second Corps staff officer, dateline Hd. Qrs. 2nd Corps A.N.V., Carlisle Pa., 'We reached here yesterday and took quiet possession of the place, quartering a portion of our forces at the U.S. Barracks ... and a portion in the ample yard of Dickinson College'; (2) 'We made requisition on the town for supplies, medicines &c and obtained some $50000 of medicines & large supplies of provisions' and 'Our success has been complete, no opposition'. That is the invasion of Pennsylvania before the battle, as the entry says ('written during the invasion'). Hotchkiss's role as the corps' topographical engineer is not stated in the letter itself and was not verified from a fetched source.
items.extraction_notes: Use the live HTML (or the TEI XML) of https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/letters/A4042. The page prints the text twice, 'Original' and 'Modern Spelling'; take only the Original, which keeps '&' and '--' as in the transcription. Two long paragraphs plus a short one and the closing (about 6 passages). No page images on the host, so the transcription cannot be checked there; the LC microfilm is the original. Cite as the site asks, with the UVA/LC credit.

items.written: 1863-06-12 to 1863-07-18 (diary entries; the surviving form is a later typed transcript of unstated date)
items.rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 diary. Isaac Harris's death year was not found; he was a young man in 1863 (his guardian O.G. Carter is mentioned), so a death after 1955 would imply an age of 110 or more, and the text itself is almost certainly out of copyright, but that is inference, not a fetched fact. Tier A2 because the only form is a typed transcript (gift of Caroline Harris Baldwin; file name I-BaldwinC-1998-1) with modern editorial footnotes by Dickinson, under the host's 'All rights reserved' footer; nothing states who made the transcript or on what terms.
items.evidence: Listed URL: 301 to https then 404 (25,372 bytes). Wayback item page 20231210113055 (22,113 bytes): 'Isaac Harris Diary, U.S. Sanitary Commission', 16 pages, Date June 12 - July 18, 1863, 'This transcript of a portion of the diary ... A complete copy of the diary transcript, with entries from June 12 through September 25, 1863, is maintained at the U.S. Army Heritage and Education Center.' PDF captures 20191118035342 (1,038,278) and 20220518060218 (1,038,307) both end at exactly 1,048,576 bytes when fetched: the file is a linearized PDF whose own header says it is 1,063,700 bytes with 16 pages, so the capture is cut by about 15 KB and has no xref (poppler refuses it). I recovered the text layer anyway by inflating every page content stream (my script tmp/sources-v2/v2b/pdftxt.py): all 16 pages (Dickinson cover plus 15 transcript pages, printed pp. 5-19) are present, including the entries of 15-18 July on printed p. 19; only the scan of the last page is cut, and the file contains no appendix (the footnote 'See inventory of USSC stores in the Appendix' refers to something not in this PDF). Description checks: (1) 'took shelter by the jail wall during the shelling': 1 July entry, Carlisle, 'I found comfortable quarters under the lee of the jail wall with Gowan, Smith and others', after Fitzhugh Lee's surrender demand was refused; the shelling lasted 'about an hour and a quarter', one militiaman (Holliday) hit; verified. (2) 'later worked with the wounded': what the text shows is relief-supply work, not care of the wounded: 6-7 July he takes stores to the hospital in Dickinson College ('Hospital which was located in Dickinson College', talks to Dr. Tomlinson, gives Mrs. Tomlinson carte blanche to buy), 10-11 July he finds about 70 Confederate patients in Chambersburg hospitals 'without supplies of any kind' and telegraphs for an outfit. Partly accurate. Also in the text: Harrisburg and Shippensburg/Chambersburg in the weeks before, the 22 June Confederate dash at Chambersburg, 5 July news of Gettysburg, and the march of the 13th Brooklyn to Boonsboro.
items.extraction_notes: Text layer recoverable from the truncated capture with a per-stream inflate script (poppler fails). Layout: page content streams interleave the transcript text with editorial footnotes that begin with '>' (for example the note on 'Knipe', 'Central Office', 'Orange Judd'): strip them, they are modern Dickinson text. OCR-style damage inside the typed text ('QJ.larters', 'dty', 'flrst', 'frre'). The page images are JBIG2 (not decoded here), so nothing was checked against an original. The diary uses racial slurs and describes the death of an enslaved or hired Black man ('Washington'); a quote selection needs careful framing. Link-out to the Wayback item page; use the text for facts and dates (Carlisle 1 July, Carlisle hospital 7 July, Chambersburg hospitals 10-11 July) only.
issues: The 1 MiB-truncated Wayback capture still holds the full text layer (all 16 pages, through printed p. 19); only the last scan is cut. The first pass said p. 19 was missing: not so for the text.
Typed transcript with modern editorial footnotes interleaved in the text stream; the original diary is not shown and may be a later transcription: no way to verify fidelity.
'Worked with the wounded' overstates what the text shows (supply and relief work, hospital visits).

items.written: Letter 1: Baltimore, July 1863 (undated beyond month); letter 2: Baltimore, 1863-08-13
items.rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 private letters. Stayman gave a commencement oration in 1841 (live Dickinson people page), so he was born around 1820 and was dead before 1956: the text itself is out of copyright (death year not fetched). items.evidence: Listed URL http://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war-people/stayman-john-keagy: 301 to https then 404 (25,343 bytes). Wayback capture 20231130070857 of that page (19,658 bytes) lists two letters, 'Letter from John K. Stayman to Edgar E. Hastings', July 1863 and August 13, 1863; it contains no biography and does not call him a professor. Item captures: 20240731222132 (6 pages, I-MachemerA-1975-1: 'describes Carlisle after the departure of Confederate troops ... a hospital being set up at the college ... entire destruction of the Army Barracks ... wounded from the Gettysburg battlefield during a stint in Philadelphia'; tags include Shelling of Carlisle) and 20240719132709 (5 pages, I-Friends-2013-3, draft and hospital). Letter 1 PDF (capture 20240630002255, 3,108,759 bytes, complete, sha256 20c7c54adbde396d...): cover plus four manuscript page images (1538x2431) and a typed transcript with text layer. Read: 'Baltimore July 1863 ... I left for a flying visit to Carlisle, to see what damage had been done by the rebel occupation and shelling. As I returned, I stopped in Philadelphia at the West Phila. Hospital ... A large number of the wounded from Gettysburg had just been received'; 'The Hospital in the College is but a temporary arrangement ... The Barracks have suffered most. They are now a heap of ruins.'; he also says he wants early news of 'the result of the Draft in Carlisle'. Comparing the first manuscript sheet with the typed text: the manuscript appears to read 'Yours of the 27th ult.' where the typed transcript prints 'Yours the 29th ult.' (my reading of a handwritten digit, flagged for a human). Letter 2: the live current-site page https://archives.dickinson.edu/document-descriptions/letter-john-k-stayman-edgar-e-hastings (HTTP 200, 30,737 bytes) is this 13 August letter, with live PDF /sites/default/files/files_document/I-Friends-2013-3_2.pdf (2,062,386 bytes, fetched; the Wayback capture of the older file is cut at 1 MiB): 'Have they begun to vacate the College as a Hospital? It is about time to do so, that the smell of puddings and poultices ... may no longer linger'; 'unfortunately the honor of being considered by Uncle Sam a first class man' (the draft). The live Stayman people page lists the August letter and an 1841 oration 'Difference of Opinion' by 'John K Stayman'; it does not list the July letter, whose PDF is not at the new paths I tried. 'Dickinson professor' is not supported by any page or letter I read; the 1841 oration makes him a Dickinson alumnus of about 40 in 1863, writing from Baltimore, with a Carlisle post-office box, who offers a Latin prize book 'for Presentation at the opening of next Session'.
items.extraction_notes: Letter 1: Wayback PDF 20240630002255 (https://web.archive.org/web/20240630002255/https://archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/files_war/I-MachemerA-1975-1.pdf), pdftotext gives a clean typed transcript of about 3,800 characters; check against the four manuscript sheets (the 27th/29th discrepancy shows the transcript is not safe unchecked). Letter 2: use the live PDF (2,062,386 bytes; text layer clean, about 1,600 characters, a short letter of 4 short paragraphs) at https://archives.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/files_document/I-Friends-2013-3_2.pdf. Segment letter 1 by paragraph: reason for the trip, Philadelphia hospital and Gettysburg wounded, Carlisle damage and hospital, draft. About 6 passages in all. Enter as two separate documents, not as one 'Stayman letters' record. Aftermath, not campaign: neither letter describes the occupation or shelling as witnessed, only its aftermath.

items.written: 1863-08-07 (dateline 'Near Orange Court House, Va., Aug 7th, 1863'; five weeks after the retreat)
items.rights_basis: Author William W. Sillers died 9 November 1863 (Notre Dame introduction, fetched via Wayback), so the unpublished 1863 letter is long out of copyright. Tier A2 because the page footer reads 'Copyright 2006, 2009, 2011 Dept. of Special Collections, University of Notre Dame', the transcription (Paul Patterson and George Rugg, 2004-06) follows documented editorial conventions and adds bracketed annotations, and no licence is stated.
items.evidence: Listed URL https://rarebooks.nd.edu/digital/civil_war/letters/sillers-holmes/5025-12.shtml: my fetch got 301, 301, then HTTP 200 on https://rarebooks.library.nd.edu/ (20,112 bytes, the Rare Books home page): a generic redirect. The same path on the new host answers 403 AccessDenied (111-byte XML), so it is not served. Wayback capture 20231211132213 (34,933 bytes) read: 'Sillers-Holmes Family Correspondence - August 7, 1863 (transcriptions only)', Autograph Letter Signed, author William W. Sillers, place Near Orange Court House, Virginia, to Frances Sillers Holmes, 4 pages, MSN/CW 5025-12. The collection index (Wayback 20240730113049) gives the author as a Confederate officer of the 30th North Carolina Infantry: private April 1861, 1st lieutenant, major from 1 May 1862 (so a major on 7 August 1863), lieutenant colonel on 3 September 1863, fought at Gettysburg on 1 July in Ramseur's brigade, Rodes's division, mortally wounded 7 November 1863. The entry's 'Confederate officer' and '30th North Carolina' are therefore right; 'letter from the campaign' is loose: this letter is written five weeks after it, from Virginia. Content: 'We drank the claret with plenty of ice in it at Carlisle Barracks in Pennsylvania ... We spent three days very pleasantly at Carlisle'; 'Genl. Fitzhugh Lee burned all these buildings down'; his servant 'Ransom fell in with a party of pillaging soldiers at Gettysburg'; the mess-chest taken 'at Waterloo Gap in Pennsylvania'; 'I have made two trips to Maryland since I was at home'. The sibling letter 5025-11 (31 July 1863, fetched) is a more direct campaign summary ('I doubt the policy of going beyond the Potomac and attacking the enemy in very strong positions') and was not listed. The collection's Technical Details page (fetched) documents spelling retained, '[illeg]', annotations in square brackets ('[i.e., ...]', '[sp. ...]'). Page images are not on Wayback at the paths tried (150/100/72 DPI JPEGs), so the transcription was not checked against the manuscript.
items.extraction_notes: HTML page (Wayback id_ capture) with the transcription in a single block; about 5,000 characters of clean text, no OCR; segment by manuscript page (headings 'Page 1 Images' to 'Page 4 Images' mark the breaks): weather and drill; clothes and his brother; the servant at Gettysburg and the sacking of dry-goods stores; Carlisle Barracks and the burning. About 5 passages. Remove the bracketed editorial interventions ('[i.e., Sgt. Robert M. Crumpler, Cpl. James M. Crumpler, and Sgt. Henry Williamson, all Co. A, 30th North Carolina Infantry]') and the navigation text. The letter speaks of 'my negroes', 'two servants' and 'Ransom' (an enslaved man who looted with soldiers in Pennsylvania): sensitive framing.

Sullivan in July, 1932, at Hereford, England ... Read before the Hamilton Library Association ... February 24, 1933, by John M. Rhey, Esq.', '1933'. No copyright notice on the title page image, and no 'copyright', '(c)' or 'all rights reserved' string anywhere in the PDF's text layer (searched); the host's footer says 'All rights reserved'. If no notice was printed the pamphlet entered the public domain on publication, but I did not view the verso or the notice-bearing pages beyond the title page and the last page, and I did not search Copyright Office renewal records; as a 1933 work it would otherwise stay protected until 1 January 2029. Needs counsel.
items.evidence: Listed URL: 301 to https then 404 (25,400 bytes). Wayback item page 20231002015237 (20,592 bytes): '"Boyhood Memories of The Civil War 1861-'65," by James W. Sullivan', 46 pages, Date July 1932, 'Publisher: Carlisle, PA: Hamilton Library Association', 'James W. Sullivan writes to Jane Van Ness Smead in July 1932 ... The Hamilton Library Association published Sullivan's letter as a pamphlet the following year', tags Invasion of Carlisle / Shelling of Carlisle / Burning of Barracks. PDF capture 20240622030747 (14,654,048 bytes, sha256 c090b254e0a63e99..., fetched complete; the CDX lists an older 1,038,573-byte capture): cover sheet, title page, 44 numbered pages, and an OCR layer of about 110,000 characters. The title page shows no publisher name other than the Hamilton Library Association seal and '1933'. Description check against the text: the memoir says 'my competency to observe ... being only ... that of a lad of fifteen', describes the Confederate cavalry entering Main Street, the infantry passing through the night of 30 June to 1 July, then 'On July 1, 1863 ... The occupation of the town by Confederates was at an end', the arrival of the 22nd and 23rd New York National Guard and a battalion of the 71st New York, the sudden shelling ('I heard the music of my first shell'), a flag of truce, the burning of the Barracks, and, afterwards, sightseers going to the Gettysburg field and Confederate prisoners. So 'a Carlisle boy who witnessed the occupation and shelling' is accurate. The writer says himself that he never found an official report and offers 'the impression of an eye-witness'.
items.extraction_notes: PDF https://web.archive.org/web/20240622030747/https://archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/files_war/SC974.8432-S949b.pdf (pdftotext works). About 25 passages in the relevant sections; check against the scan. Contains racial slurs, quoted as playmates' remarks and used by the writer in ordinary speech ('niggers', 'darky women'): handle with care. Do not ingest anything from it until counsel decides the rights tier.

summary: Second-verifier pass on entries 605, 606, 608, 609, 611, 613, 614, 617, re-derived from fetched sources. Result: 6 APPROVE (605, 608, 609, 611, 614, 617), 1 NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW (613), 1 REJECT (606). After deciding, I compared with the first-pass verdicts: all 8 verdicts, rights tiers and kinds agree, so none of these needs a human tie-break; I add details the first pass did not record (OPenn's explicit Public Domain Mark; all of 605 and 608 are image-only, so quoting needs a human transcription or OCR; the Carlisle Herald transcription deviates from its image in 3 words; the Lockwood authorship oddity; Wayback captures of 613; the source of the whole list). Every fetch used the honest Gettysburg-sources-QC User-Agent, at most 1 request/second per host, with robots.txt read first. Slower hosts: hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu has Crawl-delay: 600, so I made exactly 5 page requests to it (including robots.txt), 10 minutes apart. Perseus was not fetched. credo.library.umass.edu and nytimes.com returned bot challenges and were not circumvented. No browser was launched; nothing under legacy/, tools/t0, tests/t0, ops, baseline, release, src/lib/time, tools/time, tools/data was touched, and nothing was written to the repo. Raw fetches are in C:\Users\mlege\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mlege-AppData-Roaming-Claude-scratch-workspaces-fe20000a-2144-4d85-ac4c-4e19e62f5823-1fb796a8-22ef-47aa-b6e3-227d4048a221-scratch-2026-09-30-719300\e8c35c4e-da23-46e7-a494-c2d002ec16e2\scratchpad\v2b-second (pf.mjs is the polite fetcher; hdq2.mjs and hdq.log are the slow queue and its log).
systemic_findings: All eight entries in this batch come from one blog post: 'Beyond Gettysburg: Primary Sources for the Gettysburg Campaign' (Cooper Wingert, Blog Divided, 11 June 2018, https://housedivided.dickinson.edu/sites/blogdivided/2018/06/11/beyond-gettysburg-primary-sources-for-the-gettysburg-campaign/). The list's titles are the blog's link texts ('Anonymous Letter from Cumberland County resident', 'Richard Southeron Shreve account', 'John Lockwood memoir') and its descriptions are paraphrases of them; the Part IX header 'compiled by Dickinson College House Divided Project' is that blog post. So titles can name a person, host or label rather than a work (606, 613), and an AI-written description adds nothing beyond the link text.

hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/robots.txt carries 'Crawl-delay: 600' (comment 'Keith added for testing 8/14'; the same 2,053-byte file is already in tmp/sources-v2/cache/b604, so it was there during the earlier runs). Each page costs 10 minutes of polite fetching: 5 requests took about 50 minutes. Any re-probe of the host must honour it; the 1.2 s default is not enough there.

Image-only items are common among the best sources: 605 (handwritten diary, no transcription anywhere on OPenn) and 608 (clipping image, 'Transcription not yet available') cannot enter the verbatim corpus without a human transcription or OCR plus a second check. Host transcriptions that do exist are not verbatim: the Carlisle Herald transcription (614) differs from its own image in at least 3 words (a legible word marked illegible, two respellings) while claiming to preserve spelling; the Culver transcription (617) has bracketed guesses.

Bot-blocking is wider than eHistory and HathiTrust: credo.library.umass.edu serves a 'Security Check' page (HTTP 200) to every request, robots.txt included, and nytimes.com archive pages return HTTP 403 with a DataDome challenge. The registry's link class 'redirected (HTTP 200)' hides such a challenge for 613; the probe should flag a page title of 'Security Check' or a tiny body as blocked_to_bots.

Perseus-linked SHSP articles can be located in the Internet Archive scans: 611 is SHSP vol. 24 pp. 339-350 (archive.org/details/southernhistoric24sout, 1896 title page). IA's 'date' field there says 1876 (series start), so tier A1 should rest on the title page, not on the metadata. Note the viewer index versus page_numbers.json leaf offset (printed p. 340 is viewer page n353 and leafNum 354).

Authorship in catalogues can contradict the text: for 609 the catalogues (LoC 02010559, IA, Google, Gutenberg) name John Lockwood, but the book's first-person preface praises a comrade 'Lockwood' in the third person and the title page has no author. Cite as 'John Lockwood (catalogue attribution)'.

Entries 605, 614 and 617 describe the same event (the Carlisle shelling of 1/2 July 1863 by Fitz Lee's cavalry) from the gunner in Landis's battery, the local newspaper and a woman whose family's farm lay under the Confederate batteries; with entries 595 and 599 (Landis's report) they let the Historian cross-check the event, which is campaign-only and not Gettysburg battle content.

Of these 8 entries none describes fighting at Gettysburg except 611 (Schuricht's 1 to 3 July entries, Jenkins's brigade and the cavalry fight on the Confederate left); the rest are invasion, occupation and opinion (campaign-only). 609 reports the battle only by hearsay.

Not verified by me in this batch: the content of the Credo letter (613); the Perseus text (611); the original NYT page and date (608); the Google Books page anchors and Trout's text (606, 609); the German original of Schuricht's diary; House Divided's reuse terms (only a Creative Commons logo with no licence named on node pages and a 'Content 2007-2010 by Dickinson College' footer on the blog); University of Iowa's terms for the Culver manuscript (617); and any original issue of the Carlisle Herald (614).

items.written: Diary entries of 24 June to 2 July 1863 (the journal spans Aug 1862 to July 1863). The Carlisle entries read as a fair copy or a write-up made after the event ('as I afterwards ascertained' on fol. 62r); the date of the write-up is not stated.
items.rights_basis: OPenn item page and TEI header both carry a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark statement for the metadata and for 'these images and the content' (free of known copyright restrictions and in the public domain). Unpublished 1862-63 manuscript; author C. A. Schaeffer 1843-1898 per the OPenn summary; holder Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia (Krauth Memorial Library Archives). OPenn offers no transcription, so no host transcription right is in play.
items.extraction_notes: Image-only handwriting: 187 page images (web JPG about 300 KB each, TIFF masters; OPenn robots.txt disallows only *.tif); the HTML table of contents stops at fol. 60r (1 July 1863) and the TEI header holds no transcription. Verbatim use is therefore BLOCKED until a person transcribes fols. 59r-62r (images 1028_0118..0124) and a second person checks it (same state as entry 590). The hand is a clear copperplate. The writer is a gunner in Capt. Landis's Philadelphia artillery company, the battery of entries 595 and 599, so the entry is a first-person companion to Landis's report. The fragment #a60r works on the https page (fol. 60r is the first page of the 1 July entry); the plain-http URL in the list answers 302 to https.
issues: Title says 'University of Pennsylvania OPenn': OPenn is only the hosting platform; the manuscript belongs to the Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia (Krauth Memorial Library Archives). Author's full name is Charles Ashmead Schaeffer; the title page reads 'Journals of C. A. Schaeffer'.
Carlisle context, not Gettysburg: the entry is the evening shelling of Carlisle by Fitz Lee's cavalry on 1/2 July (flag of truce, Gen. W. F. Smith's refusal); no fighting at Gettysburg is described.
Not strictly contemporaneous: the July entry says 'afterwards ascertained' and 'I did not at the time understand', and the neat even hand suggests a fair copy; the date of writing is unknown.
The journal stops after the night of 1/2 July (fol. 62v is blank), so nothing about the battle itself or the return is in it.
Plain http in the list; the https form is needed for the anchor.
I read fols. 59v-62r and 62v (images 0119-0125) and the title page; fols. 3r-58v (Boston Treasury chemistry work and earlier entries) were not read.
items.evidence: Fetched http://openn.library.upenn.edu/Data/0010/html/00_J91_42_P4529j.html (302 to https, 200, 190,738 B, sha256 252f58bc...) and the TEI XML (73,263 B). Both licence elements point to http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/. Viewed the web JPGs: title page (0002), fol. 59v (0119: Landis's company, mustering at the armory at 18th and Market on 24 June, Harrisburg and Fort Washington, march to Carlisle on 1 July with guns and horses), fols. 60r-62r (0120-0124: arrival in Carlisle about 6 PM, market house supper, alarm about 7 PM, shells, their gun fired 3 rounds, named wounded, flag of truce to Gen. Smith with Fitz Lee's demand, ceasefire about 11:30 PM, rebels gone by about 4 AM, closing estimate of rebel strength) and fol. 62v (0125, blank). Compare with entries 614 and 617, which describe the same night.

items.written: Composed after the campaign and published 1864 (Brooklyn: A. H. Rome & Brothers); covers 15 June to about 10 July 1863

Rome & Brothers ... 1864'); IA metadata date 1864 and possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; Project Gutenberg #31258 lists 'Public domain in the USA'; LoC record 02010559 (1864, 168 p.). Not a reprint.
items.extraction_notes: Take the text from Internet Archive ourcampaignaroun00lock (NYPL scan, 186 images, DjVu text 262,636 B, sha256 5babb07a..., OCR errors present, so proofread against the page images) or from the human-proofread Project Gutenberg eBook #31258 (produced from the same IA scans). The Google Books link is the Harvard copy (id TdA_AAAAYAAJ, 168 pp., full view, same 1864 imprint); its dq=/pg=PA1 anchor was not requested (robots) and is unchecked. The appendix holds a dated itinerary (Sunday 28 June to Friday 10 July) useful for the 23rd NYSNG's movements.
issues: The title page names no author. John Lockwood (1825 or 1826-1901) comes from catalogues only (LoC 02010559, IA, Google Books, Gutenberg). The preface, in the first person, praises 'Lockwood, the upright, trusty and solid soldier' among 'my companions in arms' in the third person, which is odd if Lockwood is the author: attribution is unresolved; attribute as 'John Lockwood (catalogue attribution)'.

Title labels him '23rd NYSNG'; the book is a regimental memorial of the Brooklyn 23rd and other regiments associated with it in the emergency campaign. The 23rd was not engaged at Gettysburg (the preface itself says the militia were not in the battle); the book reports hearsay of the battle (paroled prisoners on 3 July) and the post-battle march through Cashtown (6 July) to Waynesboro.
Retrospective: written up for publication, not a diary, although it incorporates daily marching notes.
Google Books anchor not checkable (robots).

items.written: Diary of 15 June to 14 July 1863; English translation by the diarist printed in the Richmond Dispatch 5 April 1896 and reprinted in SHSP vol. 24 (1896), pp. 339-350

Brock, Richmond, Va.: Published by the Society, 1896, Wm. Ellis Jones, Printer'); IA's own 'date' field says 1876 (series start) and the item has no copyright-status field, so the title-page year is the basis.
items.extraction_notes: Use the Internet Archive scan https://archive.org/details/southernhistoric24sout (DjVu text 1,091,928 B, sha256 e06458ac...). The article starts on printed p. 339 (page_numbers.json leaf 353; the page image served as page/n353 shows printed p. 340, so printed p. 339 is viewer index n352) and the diary ends on p. 350, followed by 'A War Letter' (W. K., 30 June 1863); I read the end page from the OCR page headers. The OCR is rough in places (broken words, digits, e.g. 'tile nKjrning'), so proofread against the page images. The Perseus link was not fetched (robots Disallow: /).
issues: Listed Perseus link is robots-disallowed: not fetched, so its text and chapter anchor (2001.05.0282, chapter 1.60) are unverified; replace it with the Archive scan.
Author spelled Herman in the list; the printed article says Hermann; he signs as First Lieutenant of Company D, 14th Virginia Cavalry.

'Contemporaneous' needs a caveat: the diary was kept in German in 1863, but what is printed is a selection ('Extracts') translated by the author 33 years later for a newspaper letter about the cavalry in the Gettysburg campaign; the German original was not seen, and some entries carry hindsight ('this third day of the battle').
The article begins on printed p. 339, not at the volume's start; the article title is 'Jenkins' Brigade in the Gettysburg Campaign', not 'Schuricht diary'.
The Internet Archive date field is 1876, which is not the volume's imprint year.
items.evidence: Perseus not fetched (robots Disallow: /, also recorded by the registry). Fetched https://archive.org/metadata/southernhistoric24sout (200): title 'Southern Historical Society papers', volume 24, 408 images, Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center. Read the DjVu text: the index lists 'Schuricht, Diary of Lieutenant H.; Gettysburg Campaign, 339'; the article, headed 'Jenkins' Brigade in the Gettysburg Campaign. Extracts from the Diary of Lieutenant Hermann Schuricht, of the Fourteenth Virginia Cavalry' [From the Richmond Dispatch, April 5, 1896], opens with his letter of 1 April 1896 offering a translation of his diary from 15 June (crossing the Potomac) to 14 July. Entries checked: 27 June (brigade occupies Carlisle), 28 June (Mechanicsburg, artillery fire near Harrisburg), 1 July (heard the cannonading from the road to Gettysburg), 2 July (Jenkins's brigade posted on the first day's field, Jenkins wounded by a shell), 3 July (cavalry fight on the Confederate left, a lieutenant killed beside him), 14 July (last troops to leave Maryland). Viewed the scan image of printed p. 340 (leaf n353): clean 1896 print matching the OCR. Description (diary of a Confederate cavalry officer in Jenkins's brigade, printed in SHSP) is accurate.

items.extraction_notes: I could not read the letter: every request to credo.library.umass.edu (the page, and robots.txt itself) returns HTTP 200 with a 3,144-byte 'Security Check' page, which I did not try to pass. The Digital Commonwealth item page is reachable and shows the metadata and an abstract only; the images are served from hosts that disallow bots (iiif.digitalcommonwealth.org robots: Disallow: /; Digital Commonwealth disallows /downloads/). A human must open the Credo page in a browser, read the 4-page manuscript, decide whether the writer is in Cumberland County, and ask UMass about quotation before any text is used. There is no transcription in the record.
issues: Could not read the document; description unverified beyond the repository abstract.

Listed title 'Anonymous letter from a Cumberland County resident' is the blog's link text. The repository calls it 'Letter from unidentified correspondent to Sidney Boden', 11 July 1863, 4 p., Burgett-Irey Family Papers (UMass Amherst); it gives no place of writing, and Carlisle appears in the abstract only as a place others had visited ('a day or two after they left Carlisle'), so 'Cumberland County' is unverified.
Registry probe recorded 'redirected (HTTP 200)' for this link, which hides the bot challenge.

Wayback Machine holds only 3 captures of the page (CDX: 2020-02-03 HTTP 302, 2024-07-07 HTTP 302, 2026-05-12 HTTP 200 of 2,012 bytes, consistent with a challenge page), so there is no readable archived copy.
Reuse requires a request to the repository; no licence.
items.evidence: Fetched http://credo.library.umass.edu/view/full/mums605-s02-b006-i009 (308 to https, 200, 3,144 B, title 'Security Check'); same for https://credo.library.umass.edu/robots.txt. Identity established elsewhere: Digital Commonwealth robots.txt allows /search.json and /search/<id> (Crawl-Delay 5 honoured). The search.json record commonwealth-oai:ff36c7412 has identifier mums605-s02-b006-i009, URI https://credo.library.umass.edu/view/full/mums605-s02-b006-i009, title 'Letter from unidentified correspondent to Sidney Boden', date 11 July 1863, addressee Sidney Boden, extent 4 p., collection Burgett-Irey Family Papers, 1832-2012, UMass Amherst Special Collections and University Archives. Its abstract: mail service suspended because of the war, rebel forces came into the area without resistance, valuables should be hidden, armed men asked at the door if there were abolitionists, cavalry and infantry filling the roads, Marion Weakley visited a day or two after they left Carlisle. That abstract matches 'civilian letter describing the invasion'. The item page (27,222 B) fetched too. Wayback availability and CDX queries (archive.org, after a 429 back-off) gave the three captures listed above.

items.written: 1863-07-10 (Carlisle Herald, p. 2, col. 5), nine days after the shelling it describes
items.rights_basis: Underlying text: 1863 US newspaper (pre-1931 imprint, date from the host's citation). The host's transcription (transcriber Don Sailer, 3 May 2011) claims to preserve spelling and typographical errors but does not, and its footer shows a Creative Commons logo with no licence named; no reuse terms found. The clipping image is low-resolution and partly unreadable, so the text would in practice come from the host's transcription.
items.extraction_notes: Do not ingest the host transcription verbatim. Compared with the clipping image I found at least four differences: the image reads 'the residue formed the best line of defence' where the transcription has '[illegible]' and 'defense'; 'the defenceless women' is respelled 'defenseless'; the image reads 'eternal infamy await' where the transcription has 'awaits'. A human must read the image (369 x 982 px, sha256 105fde9a...; partly blurred in the lower third) or obtain a better scan of the Carlisle Herald of 10 July 1863 (not found by me), after which the text would be A1. The listed http URL redirects to https per the registry probe; I requested the https form only (host Crawl-delay 600 s).
issues: The piece is a short local editorial paragraph, not a witness account: it is partisan (it praises citizen skirmishers at Letort Spring and calls Fitz Lee names) and its claim that citizens beat back the rebel advance is not corroborated by other accounts I read (Culver and Schaeffer describe artillery exchanges only).
Host transcription is not verbatim despite its own statement (3 or more deviations from the image) and has an '[illegible]' for a legible word.
Clipping carries no date line; date and column come from the host citation.
House Divided reuse terms not found (Creative Commons logo only).
items.evidence: Fetched https://hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/node/33707 (200, 37,674 B, sha256 66e154ec...) after the 10-minute crawl delay. Record: 'Carlisle (PA) Herald, "Behavior of Our Citizens Under Rebel Fire," July 10, 1863, p. 2: 5', Date Certainty Exact, transcriber Don Sailer, Dickinson College, 05/03/2011, one paragraph (about 300 words), event link 'Shells from General J.E.B. Stuart's horse artillery rain down on Carlisle in an evening bombardment', people Fitzhugh Lee and W. F. Smith. The text says about three thousand militia under Gen. Smith, a flag of truce demanding surrender, refusal, shelling, troops ordered into houses, citizens forming a skirmish line at Letort Spring. Downloaded and viewed the clipping image 1863_07_10_citzens.jpg (261,422 B) and compared the words listed in extraction notes. Description 'local newspaper account of Carlisle residents during the shelling' is accurate.

items.written: 1863-07-09 (letter headed 'East Villa July 9th /63', written from Carlisle)
items.rights_basis: Letter of 1863 by a private writer (Hanna Culver); the underlying manuscript is held by the University of Iowa Special Collections (Joseph Franklin Culver collection), terms not found. The text is House Divided's own 2018 transcription (PDF made in Apple Pages, 3 July 2018) with uncertain readings in brackets and no page images; Blog Divided's footer reads 'Content 2007-2010 by Dickinson College'. No licence found for either the transcription or the manuscript.
items.extraction_notes: Text layer is clean (2 pages, 3,917 + 2,598 characters, extracted with pypdf). Uncertain readings are marked with [?] and [Burg?]; the transcription has no page images, so quote only after checking the Iowa manuscript images (ask University of Iowa Special Collections) and resolving rights (tier A2: hold:rights-review). Host: housedivided.dickinson.edu has no robots.txt (404); the listed http URL answered 301 to https and then 200 as an application/pdf.
issues: Rights: host transcription of a manuscript held by Iowa; terms not found for either.
Uncertain readings in brackets; the transcription cannot be treated as verbatim.
Spelling Hanna in the PDF and the list; the Iowa blog writes 'Sister Hannah'.

Mixes the occupation and the shelling with second-hand news of the battle ('so badly beaten at Gettiesburg', family members gone to see the field); nothing is an eyewitness account of the Gettysburg fighting.
items.evidence: Fetched http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/sites/blogdivided/files/2018/06/HannaCulver-1.pdf (301 to https, 200, application/pdf, 49,732 B, sha256 bd2c3776...) and extracted the text. Caption: 'Hanna Culver from Carlisle to her brother Joseph F. Culver, Joseph Franklin Culver collection, Special Collection, University of Iowa library. Her brother was serving with the 129th Illinois Infantry in Tennessee.' Letter dated 9 July 1863: Jenkins's advance entered Carlisle on a Saturday morning, Ewell's division was arriving by 3 PM with a supply train three miles long, foraging and the sacking of stores, Ewell's corps leaving on the Baltimore pike on Tuesday, then Gen. Smith's brigade on Wednesday evening, shells, a flag of truce from Fitzhugh Lee, a cannonade of about four hours with batteries near her house, the Gas Works and the garrison set on fire, 17 Union soldiers wounded, two amputations. Matches entries 605 and 614 on the shelling. Identity cross-checks: Blog Divided post 'Beyond Gettysburg' (11 June 2018) lists it as Culver Family Correspondence ('Hanna Culver's July 9, 1863 letter detailing the occupation and shelling'); the University of Iowa Culver letters blog (blog.lib.uiowa.edu/culver, robots allowed) shows Joseph F. Culver of the 129th Illinois writing to his wife about 'Sister Hannah' and the family in Carlisle (post of 19 Aug 1863).
